name: Curaçao Papiamentu
catalog_citation: Remijsen, Bert & Vincent J. van Heuven. 2005. Stress, tone and discourse prominence in the Curaçao dialect of Papiamentu. Phonology 22: 205-235. doi:10.1017/S0952675705000540 (Leiden repository postprint, hdl.handle.net/1887/14092, fetched sources via Wayback)
catalog_quote: Curaçao Papiamentu has both lexically distinctive stress and, independently, a word-level tone contrast. ... In verbs, the location of primary stress is predictable from the number of syllables and the morphological category. The vast majority of disyllabic verbs have penultimate stress in the base form. ... In the corresponding participle forms (1b), however, stress is on the final syllable. ... Longer verbs uniformly have final stress, both in the base form and in the participle ... In nouns, adjectives and adverbs – i.e. in all lexical categories other than verbs – stress is to some extent predictable from syllable weight, with closed syllables counting as heavy. That is, stress is on the penultimate, unless the final syllable is heavy, in which case the final syllable is stressed, as shown in (2). ... However, there are many exceptions to this weight-sensitive stress rule – see the …
sweep_summary: Papiamento (papi1253) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Remijsen & van Heuven 2005. The sweep list holds three distinct works (seven Glottolog records, all already listed). (1) Remijsen & van Heuven 2005: fetched sources the open Leiden postprint (hdl:1887/14092) and read §2.2.1-2.2.3; the catalog quote is verbatim from p. 207 and the paper states stress is lexically distinctive (disyllabic verb base penult vs participle final; non-verbs weight-sensitive penult/final with many irregular final/penult/antepenult exceptions) — confirms. (2) Kouwenberg 2007 (already on file, OA): pronoun-clitic paper whose §2.2 restates the system as category-predictable (verbs final H, 3+-syllable verbs final stress, disyllabic verbs trochaic penult stress with final H; non-verbs quantity-sensitive right-edge trochee) — refines, consistent with the catalog. (3) Rivera-Castillo 1998 (JPCL 13(2): 297-334): closed at John Benjamins (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2 all closed, no repository copy); only the publisher's first-page preview image (title + abstract) was obtainable and saved; the abstract claims four basic lexical patterns of tone and stress with stress dependent on tone; Kouwenberg 2004 (pp. 61-62, Table 4) and R&vH 2005 (p. 211) summarize it as requiring lexical H placement and an independent stress prosodeme — consistent with 'lexical', medium acquisition priority since R&vH 2005 already supersedes it. Extra: Kouwenberg 2004 (on file, OA, not a sweep item) read for its Table 1 and 'Stress placement in verbs' section — refines. No source contradicts the catalog; best statement remains R&vH 2005 §2.2.1, now verified from a saved copy. access checks were done to automated fetch, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref APIs.

new_statements.reading: Curaçao Papiamentu word stress is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs 'mata 'to kill' vs ma'ta 'killed'; irregular nouns 'hoben, li'he, 'aguila) but largely rule-governed within categories: disyllabic verbs penult (participle final), verbs of 3+ syllables final; non-verbs penult unless the final syllable is closed, with many lexifier-inherited exceptions including antepenult. Secondary stress alternates from the primary. This is the catalog's deciding source, now verified first-hand from the open Leiden postprint; the catalog_quote is verbatim from p. 207 and the 'lexical' coding stands.

sources.note: Curaçao Papiamentu has lexically distinctive stress and, independently, a privative word-level tone contrast. Verbs: disyllabic base = penult stress, participle = final stress (mata/matá), 3+ syllables final in both. Non-verbs: weight-sensitive (penult unless final syllable closed), with many lexifier-inherited exceptions (final, penult, antepenult: 'hoben, li'he, 'aguila). Secondary stress on alternating syllables. §2.2.3: 'Stress is distinctive in most disyllabic verbs, where it distinguishes the base form from the participle.' The catalog_quote is verbatim from p. 207.

sources.citation: Kouwenberg, Silvia. 2007. The prosody-syntax interface and the status of pronouns in Papiamentu. Journal of Portuguese Linguistics 6(2): 203-225. doi:10.5334/jpl.150 (open access) [Glottolog ref 680667]
sources.quote: Restates verb stress facts (bisyllabic verbs initial stress with final H; longer verbs final stress) and treats enclitic-triggered 'stress shift' (buska > buska-mi with final stress on the verb) as a surface effect of prosodic-word formation; otherwise about clitic syntax, not word-stress placement.
sources.locator: txt l.244-245, 286-289 (verbs of 3+ syllables 'always H-toned and stressed on the final syllable'; orthographic acute reflects 'a false assumption, namely that Pp's stress rules are similar to those of Spanish'); l.365-372 on apparent stress shift under object enclitics
sources.note: Main topic is pronoun cliticisation, but §2.2 restates the word-prosodic system: H tone is category-predictable (verbs final H; non-verbs weight-sensitive trochaic footing from the right edge), stress coincides with H except in disyllabic verbs where the trochaic foot puts stress on the penult while H is final; verbs of 3+ syllables are stressed finally; object-clitic encliticisation on disyllabic verbs yields surface 'stress shift' to the final syllable (pp. 213-215). Fn. 8 (citing Kouwenberg 2004:56) says the orthography wrongly treats predictable final verb stress as exceptional Spanish-ty…

sources.citation: Kouwenberg, Silvia (2004). The grammatical function of Papiamentu tone. Journal of Portuguese Linguistics 3(2): 55-69. doi:10.5334/jpl.11 [not in the sweep item list; already on file in the audit folder, read because it is the descriptive source R&vH 2005 §2.2.1 builds on]
sources.quote: 'Traditionally, stress placement in Pp has been assumed to conform to a Spanish pattern ... Pp verbs three or more syllables long ... all end in a stress-bearing open syllable ... The fully predictable nature of high tone and stress placement in verbs ... the bisyllabic verb base combines penultimate stress with a LH melody, whereas the trisyllabic derived verb has a final stressed and high-toned syllable' (pp.56-57); 'in nouns, adjectives, and adverbs, stress placement is sensitive to the weight of the final syllable' (p.57; final schwa+/l,r,n/ counts light: binager, òrgel penult vs fabor, os
sources.locator: pp.56-59, 'Regular tone and stress placement' + Table 1 (after Kouwenberg & Murray 1994:12) and 'Irregular tone and stress placement' + Table 2
sources.note: Table 1 (after Kouwenberg & Murray 1994:12): disyllabic verbs final H + penult stress; longer verbs final H + final stress; non-verbs with heavy final syllable final H + final stress, light final syllable penult H + penult stress. Participles (matá) and some nouns (piská, ágila, difísil) are irregular and carry a lexically pre-associated H that attracts stress. Argues stress/tone are largely predictable from category and weight, with a closed set of lexically marked exceptions.

sources.quote: The description of the interdependence of tonal and stress features in Papiamentu provides important insights on the genesis of mixed creole systems in which these suprasegmental features are phonologically distinctive. The present account represents a constraint-based and feature-based analysis that [...] proposes that tone and stress are directly related. This paper includes (a) a description of four basic lexical patterns of tone and stress in Papiamentu, (b) a discussion of problems that alternative analyses face when dealing with mixed systems, and (c) a principled way to explain relations between suprasegmental features.
sources.note: The main formal (OT, foot-based) analysis of Papiamentu stress placement, summarized second-hand in Kouwenberg 2004 Table 4; relevant if the record's 'lexical vs weight-predictable' framing is ever contested.
